source.title: Quadratic integrate-and-fire neurons exhibit less fragmented loss landscapes and outperform leaky integrate-and-fire neurons in spike-based gradient descent
source.authors: Carlo Wenig; Raoul-Martin Memmesheimer; Christian Klos

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests natural-label generalization and loss/gradient behavior in spiking neural networks, a setting not covered by the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study does not test random-label memorization, interpolation-width behavior, convolutional versus fully connected networks, optimizer or batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Its SHD test-accuracy comparisons and measured loss/gradient properties bear on the claim's subject but do not fit a listed version. Hyperparameter-search results are reported in figures and tables; only selected models and explicitly described comparisons are recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study compares QIF and LIF spiking networks on spoken-digit classification and examines training-loss continuity and gradient informativeness. These results test none of V1–V8. Natural-label accuracy alone does not test V1, larger selected architectures do not establish V2's post-interpolation width trend, and landscape fragmentation does not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or its association with generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find that QIF networks outperform LIF networks in the tested SHD setup and exhibit less severe landscape fragmentation and more informative gradients. They recommend neurons with continuous spiking dynamics for gradient-based SNN training, while explicitly leaving extension beyond this task, coding scheme, oscillating-neuron regime and instantaneous-current setup for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Exact spike-based gradient descent on spiking neural networks with QIF and LIF neurons, tested on spoken-digit classification; not the listed ANN experiments or their interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Neuron type and output-spike distinctness affect test accuracy and landscape behavior; the paper focuses on one task, time-to-first-spike coding, intrinsically oscillating neurons, and infinitesimally short input currents.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected QIF networks outperform selected LIF networks on SHD: final test accuracies are 90.1% versus 79.2% for the smaller best models, and 91.3% versus 85.2% for exploratory larger models. The asynchronous LIF model reaches 50.8%. Test data informed model selection.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested SHD recipe with exact spike-based gradients, selected QIF networks achieve higher classification accuracy than selected LIF networks.

fits_no_version.finding: QIF loss landscapes have sharp continuous transitions and less fragmented gradients; LIF loss and gradients exhibit discontinuities. Expected loss decreases occur in practice for 90%, 75% and 62% of relevant updates in the QIF, best LIF and asynchronous LIF realizations, respectively. About 25% of gradient components vanish across an epoch in both best models, versus about 62% in asynchronous LIF.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this setup, QIF dynamics yield less fragmented landscapes and more predictive update gradients than LIF dynamics; these measurements concern trainability rather than magnitude-aware sharpness tracking generalization gaps.

record.code_released: not stated; the text says code will be made available upon publication.
record.problems: The authors note the study focuses on a single task and output coding scheme, intrinsically oscillating neurons, and input currents that cause jumps in membrane potential. Test data were used for hyperparameter/model selection, which the authors say may overestimate accuracy on new data. Landscape evidence is qualitative and depends strongly on the selected parameter-space slice. Large-network experiments are exploratory.
record.rows_left_out: The rough and fine hyperparameter-search grids are shown in Figures 6–10 and include many configurations; individual figure-only configurations are omitted because the flattened text does not reliably map all values to settings. The text notes the searches used test accuracy for model selection. Additional landscape plots in Figures 14–15 are not separately rowed because they add examples of the same qualitative landscape comparison.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test-error behavior as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification, local connectivity, and initialization or sparsity qualifications.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization and its dependence on tuning, weight decay or switching optimizers. Adam is used without an optimizer comparison.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce their penalty. Batch size is fixed at 1,000.
Effects of adding or removing dropout, including interactions with training-set size, augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus random examples and measuring test accuracy after retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T3 classification is incorrect: a new setting qualifies only when its results bear on a listed version. The paper briefly cites flat-minima generalization work but neither tests nor operationally relies on V1–V8. All row states are cannot_determine relative to those versions; this does not dispute the reported measurements. No omitted result bearing on a listed version was found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Width sweep past interpolation and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Large- versus small-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects across training-set sizes and augmentation settings.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal and retraining of memorized examples.

rows.subject: QIF (best)
rows.stage_stated: trained model; landscape evaluated in region relevant for learning
rows.operation_detail: Compared sample and batch loss and gradient-angle landscapes.
rows.value: QIF sample gradients have discontinuities but are less fragmented; batch gradients appear less noisy than LIF, and batch loss appears visually smooth.
rows.note: The study describes landscapes qualitatively; it does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness in V7.
rows.check: The qualitative description is supported, but the landscapes cover regions along 200-epoch training trajectories, not just a trained endpoint. Fragmentation and gradient directions do not measure V7.

rows.stage_stated: trained model; landscape evaluated in region relevant for learning
rows.operation_detail: Compared sample and batch loss and gradient-angle landscapes.
rows.value: Sample loss has discontinuous jumps; sample and batch gradients are more fragmented and erratic than QIF.
rows.note: This is a qualitative comparison, not a magnitude-aware sharpness test.
rows.check: The qualitative description is supported, but the landscapes cover regions along 200-epoch training trajectories. Loss discontinuities and erratic gradients do not measure V7.

rows.subject: QIF (best)

rows.note: Authors say the gradient is more informative for training in QIF networks.
